design_detail: Single-site, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-arm randomized trial (1:1, fixed blocks of 4) at the San Francisco Department of Public Health, 5 September 2007 to 4 March 2010. 60 sexually active men who have sex with men (MSM) with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence and a methamphetamine-positive urine at screening received mirtazapine (15 mg nightly for 1 week, then 30 mg) or matched placebo for 12 weeks, with weekly 30-minute manual-based counselling (cognitive behavioural therapy and motivational interviewing) and weekly urine tests. Primary analysis: GEE log-link model of diverging linear trends in weekly urine positivity (week 1 omitted). ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00497081.
can_establish: Whether, among actively using, non-depressed MSM receiving weekly counselling, 12 weeks of mirtazapine reduced the proportion of methamphetamine-positive weekly urine tests compared with placebo, and its short-term tolerability in 60 men.
cannot_establish: Whether mirtazapine produces abstinence (the trial was not designed for it), whether any effect persists after treatment stops or beyond 12 weeks, whether it works in women, in people with major depression or outside this MSM population, or whether the reported reductions in self-reported sexual risk translate into fewer HIV or STI infections (not measured).

sample.recruitment: Community and clinic recruitment of MSM: STD and HIV clinics, bars, community-based organizations, flyers and websites, plus peer recruitment; telephone screen, then two in-person screening visits. Participants were paid 10 dollars per weekly visit and 35 dollars for screening, baseline and 4-, 8- and 12-week visits (Methods › Study recruitment; Randomization and study procedures).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: MSM aged 18 to 60 with SCID-diagnosed DSM-IV-TR methamphetamine dependence, interest in reducing or stopping use, self-reported anal sex with men while using methamphetamine in the past 3 months, a methamphetamine-positive urine at screening, no acute medical or psychiatric illness and acceptable safety laboratory results. Excluded: current major depression (SCID), antidepressant use in the past 4 weeks, CD4 count below 200 per microlitre in people with HIV. The registry also lists bipolar disorder or psychosis, other psychotropic medication, pseudoephedrine use, liver or renal impairment and concurrent research participation.
sample.demographics: Mean age 40.5 years (SD 9.0); 62% White, 18% African American, 12% Latino, 8% other; 53% HIV-positive (16 per arm); 60% not employed; 62% with annual income below 20,000 dollars. Methamphetamine use 2 days a week or less in 40%, 3 to 6 days in 43%, daily in 17%; 68% used during sex more than half the time; routes: smoked 85%, injected 45%, snorted 40%, rectal 30%, oral 17%. Mean CES-D 16.7 (Table 1).
sample.attrition: 56 of 60 (93%) completed the final visit, 28 per arm; 4 dropped out between enrolment and week 3. 673 of 780 weekly urine samples (86%) were collected; 227 of 240 monthly visits (94.6%) were completed (Results › Participation and retention). Two participants (both randomized to mirtazapine) were found after randomization to have been taking excluded psychiatric medications.
sample.selection_effects: Of 212 people assessed in person, 72 were eligible and 60 enrolled; 44 were excluded for not meeting SCID dependence criteria and 22 for major depression. The sample is MSM only, non-depressed, motivated to cut down, paid for visits and seen weekly, so it is a selected, high-contact trial population; the authors restrict the generalization to MSM.

exposure.measurement: Assigned study medication: mirtazapine 15 mg capsules or identical placebo prepared off site, dispensed in sequentially numbered MEMS-capped bottles; one capsule nightly for week 1, then two (30 mg) nightly to week 12. Adherence by MEMS (distinct days opened divided by expected doses) and by the AIDS Clinical Trials Group self-report measure.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as above (oral, nightly, 12 weeks). Adherence was 48.5% by MEMS (48.3% mirtazapine, 48.7% placebo) and 74.7% by self-report; 10 participants on mirtazapine (33%) and 7 on placebo (23%) stopped medication for at least a week.
exposure.polysubstance: Other drug use was not an exclusion criterion and is not reported; drug use was assessed by audio computer-assisted self-interview, but no results for other substances (or for self-reported methamphetamine use) are presented.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: participants were actively using at entry (70% urine-positive at baseline) and the outcome is urine positivity during treatment.

comparison.controls: Identical-appearing placebo capsules on the same schedule, with the same weekly counselling, adherence counselling, HIV risk-reduction counselling and visit payments.
comparison.matching: Randomization by the study statistician (fixed block size 4); allocation known only to the statistician and the off-site pharmacist, neither with participant contact. Baseline imbalances: wanting counselling as a reason to join, 53% mirtazapine vs 23% placebo (p = .03); income of at least 40,000 dollars 27% vs 7%; full-time work 27% vs 10%; Severity of Dependence Scale 6.4 vs 4.9 (p = .07); receptive unprotected anal sex partners (p = .049). Sensitivity analyses adjusted for the imbalanced variables.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same population; not reported for either arm.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: methamphetamine metabolite in weekly urine (rapid immunochromatographic test). Secondary: adherence (MEMS, self-report) and sexual risk behaviour by audio computer-assisted self-interview (numbers of male partners, partners with whom methamphetamine was used, anal sex and unprotected anal sex episodes with serodiscordant partners, insertive and receptive). Also CES-D depressive symptoms, adverse events by weekly inquiry and safety laboratory tests, and an end-of-study guess of assignment.
outcomes.validity_norms: Urine testing is objective but qualitative (positive or negative) and reflects use within a detection window of days; the trial did not measure abstinence, quantity of use or self-reported use days. Sexual behaviour is self-reported over the past 4 weeks, with highly skewed counts (for example, placebo male partners at week 12: mean 24.8, SD 94.4).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit is a faster decline in the probability of a methamphetamine-positive weekly urine in the mirtazapine arm, expressed as a relative risk at 12 weeks from fitted linear trends; harm is the incidence of adverse events by arm.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 9 counts the primary urine outcome, six sexual-behaviour outcomes, CES-D and adherence; adverse events were compared by Fisher's exact test without correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind: participants and staff unaware of assignment; the registry lists participant, care provider, investigator and outcome assessor as masked. At the end, 50% of the placebo arm and 56% of the mirtazapine arm guessed their assignment correctly (p = .79), although drowsiness was reported only on mirtazapine (43%).

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary (intention-to-treat GEE, log link, robust SEs, linear time trends by arm, week 1 omitted): relative risk of a positive urine at 12 weeks, mirtazapine versus placebo, 0.57 (95% CI 0.35 to 0.93), p = .02; number needed to treat for a negative weekly urine 3.1 (as reported). Raw urine positivity: mirtazapine 22 of 30 (73%) at baseline to 12 of 27 (44%) at the final visit; placebo 20 of 30 (67%) to 17 of 27 (63%). Editors' calculation for the final visit alone (cross-sectional, unadjusted): risk difference -18.5 percentage points (95% CI -44.7 to 7.6), risk ratio 0.71 (0.42 to 1.18), corresponding to a number needed to treat of about 5.4. Sensitivity analyses: including week 1, RR 0.58 (0.38 to 0.90); missing samples imputed positive, 0.62 (0.42 to 0.93); adjusted for baseline imbalance, 0.53 (0.32 to 0.89); excluding two ineligible participants, 0.57 (0.34 to 0.93); as-treated at mean adherence, 54% reduction (21% to 74%). Sexual risk (adjusted risk ratios, mirtazapine versus placebo): partners with whom methamphetamine was used 0.45 (0.24 to 0.82); male partners 0.20 (0.04 to 0.93); anal sex with serodiscordant partners 0.31 (0.14 to 0.66); unprotected anal sex with serodiscordant partners 0.34 (0.17 to 0.70); insertive unprotected 0.29 (0.14 to 0.58); receptive unprotected 0.27 (0.05 to 1.57), p = .14. CES-D: difference between arms 1.5 points (-3.7 to 6.7), p = .57.
analysis.covariates: None in the primary model; sensitivity models adjusted for imbalanced baseline variables and for baseline correlates of missing or positive urine samples; sexual-behaviour estimates adjusted for the counselling-motivation variable and its interaction with time.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00497081, first submitted 5 July 2007, before enrolment began on 5 September 2007. The original record (version 0) described a pilot study whose primary outcomes were feasibility, tolerability (adverse events, mislabelled as an aripiprazole-versus-placebo comparison) and acceptability (adherence), with efficacy on urine results and self-reported methamphetamine use listed as the first specific aim in the detailed description. On 19 February 2008, during recruitment, the primary outcomes were changed to efficacy in reducing methamphetamine use, adherence and safety, the summary was rewritten from a feasibility pilot to an efficacy study, and masking changed from double to quadruple. With results posting on 15 October 2014 the efficacy outcome was respecified as change in the number of positive urine tests from baseline to week 12. Sexual risk behaviour and depression, reported in the paper as outcomes, were never registered; the linear-trend GEE model omitting week 1, described in the paper as prespecified, does not appear in the registry. Self-reported methamphetamine use, named in the original aim, is not reported in the paper.
analysis.selective_reporting: Self-reported methamphetamine use (collected by audio computer-assisted self-interview and named in the registered aims) and other drug use are not reported. The adverse-event inquiry criteria are 'available upon request'. The registry's posted results give 109 adverse events on mirtazapine and 107 on placebo and one serious event per arm.
analysis.power: Planned at 80% power for net reductions of 14 to 33 percentage points in urine positivity, assuming 8 of 12 samples available, 70% to 90% placebo positivity and within-person correlation of 0.5 to 0.9. Observed: 14% missing samples, 63% to 67% placebo positivity, correlation 0.45. The authors compare an observed 43% (a relative reduction) with the detectable 14 to 33 percentage points (absolute), which are different scales.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 60 non-depressed MSM receiving weekly counselling, the modelled probability of a methamphetamine-positive weekly urine fell faster on mirtazapine than on placebo (RR 0.57 at 12 weeks, 0.35 to 0.93), robust to several sensitivity analyses; at the final visit, 44% versus 63% of samples were positive, a difference that on its own is not statistically clear (editors' RR 0.71, 0.42 to 1.18). Most participants on mirtazapine were still testing positive at the end. Self-reported sexual risk measures fell more on mirtazapine. Adherence by electronic caps was under 50% in both arms. Drowsiness (43%), increased appetite and weight gain (up to 12.5 kg) occurred only on mirtazapine.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Comment state that mirtazapine decreased methamphetamine use and that the trial showed efficacy, and the abstract gives a number needed to treat of 3.1, which comes from the fitted trend model and cannot be reproduced from the printed counts (the raw final-visit difference implies about 5.4). The Comment calls the reductions in sexual risk suggestive of a causal pathway and mirtazapine a possibly effective HIV prevention intervention, although no infections were measured and the sexual outcomes were not registered. It describes mirtazapine as safe and well tolerated while noting drowsiness, appetite increase and weight gain confined to the mirtazapine arm, which the abstract summarizes as no significant differences in adverse events by arm. The paper is candid that the sample was small, MSM only and short-term and that replication is needed.

timeline.event: Kongsakon et al.: placebo-controlled pilot of mirtazapine in 20 men in a Thai probation detoxification centre, reduced withdrawal symptoms at 2 weeks (cited as the rationale).
Cruickshank et al.: mirtazapine for methamphetamine withdrawal, no difference in retention or withdrawal (cited as inconclusive).
This trial: 60 MSM, RR 0.57 for a positive urine at 12 weeks.

Coffin et al.: larger replication in 120 cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men over 24 weeks with 12 weeks of follow-up (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01888835), from an overlapping investigator team at the same health department.
Siefried et al. systematic review lists this trial among 43 and counts mirtazapine among the less consistent signals.

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of effect on urine positivity was reproduced by the larger 2020 trial in a similar population by an overlapping team, so the two are not fully independent and both are restricted to people who have sex with men; no trial in other populations had been identified in this reading. Abstinence, durability after stopping, and effects in women or in people with depression remain untested here.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant R01-DA022155 (first author); the funder had no role in design, conduct, analysis, writing or approval.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the San Francisco Department of Public Health, the University of California San Francisco and the University of California Los Angeles. The trial was run by the health department, whose staff also delivered the counselling. No industry involvement is reported.

what_would_settle_it: A multi-site, adequately powered placebo-controlled trial of mirtazapine in a broader population (including women, heterosexual men and people with depression), with a registered primary outcome on urine-verified use or abstinence over the whole treatment period, observed or biologically verified adherence, follow-up for at least 6 months after stopping, and HIV or STI incidence as an outcome if the prevention claim is to be tested.

domains.note: Statistician-generated sequence in blocks of 4; allocation concealed by an off-site pharmacist with sequentially numbered bottles; baseline imbalances (motivation for counselling, income, employment, dependence severity) consistent with chance in 60 people and adjusted in sensitivity analyses without changing the result.

Double-blind with identical capsules and an intention-to-treat analysis; equal (low) adherence in both arms; end-of-study guesses no better than chance despite drowsiness on mirtazapine; two ineligible participants (both on mirtazapine) excluded in a sensitivity analysis without change.

86% of weekly urines collected and 93% completed; imputing all missing samples as positive gave RR 0.62 (0.42 to 0.93). The per-arm collection percentages are printed inconsistently with the counts (see reporting issues).
Objective urine testing applied identically in both arms; for the self-reported sexual-behaviour outcomes the judgment would be some concerns (skewed self-reported counts).

Registered before enrolment as a feasibility pilot; primary outcomes changed to efficacy during recruitment (February 2008), apparently while blinded; the specific trend model omitting week 1 is not in the registry; self-reported methamphetamine use named in the registered aims is unreported, and the sexual-behaviour outcomes were never registered.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-concealed, double-blind trial with high retention and an objective outcome, whose main result survives conservative imputation and covariate adjustment. The concerns are about the reported result rather than its conduct: the registered primary outcome changed from feasibility to efficacy after enrolment had started, the modelling choice that produces the headline estimate cannot be checked against a registered plan, and a registered self-report outcome is missing. These do not make the urine result implausible, but they mean its magnitude (RR 0.57, NNT 3.1) should be cited as model-based and from one small trial.

key_findings.finding: 60 MSM with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence were randomized 30:30; 56 (93%, 28 per arm) completed the final visit; 673 of 780 weekly urines (86%) were collected.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Results › Participation and retention

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome (intention to treat): the risk of a methamphetamine-positive weekly urine declined faster on mirtazapine than placebo, RR 0.57 (95% CI 0.35 to 0.93) at 12 weeks, p = .02; reported number needed to treat 3.1 for a negative weekly urine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary outcome: urinalysis results, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Model-based estimate from group-specific linear trends with week 1 omitted; the NNT cannot be reproduced from the printed counts.

key_findings.finding: Raw urine positivity: mirtazapine 22 of 30 (73%) at baseline and 12 of 27 (44%) at the final visit; placebo 20 of 30 (67%) and 17 of 27 (63%). Editors' calculation for the final visit alone: risk difference -18.5 percentage points (95% CI -44.7 to 7.6), risk ratio 0.71 (0.42 to 1.18).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Results › Primary outcome, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses: including week 1, RR 0.58 (0.38 to 0.90); missing urines imputed positive, 0.62 (0.42 to 0.93); adjusted for imbalanced baseline characteristics, 0.53 (0.32 to 0.89); controlling for baseline correlates of missing or positive samples, p < .04; excluding two ineligible participants, 0.57 (0.34 to 0.93); as-treated at mean adherence, 54% reduction (21% to 74%).

Adherence was 48.5% by MEMS (48.3% mirtazapine, 48.7% placebo; p = .82) and 74.7% by self-report (75.9% vs 73.5%; p = .92); 33% on mirtazapine and 23% on placebo stopped medication for at least a week.

Self-reported sexual risk fell more on mirtazapine (adjusted risk ratios): partners with whom methamphetamine was used 0.45 (0.24 to 0.82); male partners 0.20 (0.04 to 0.93); anal sex with serodiscordant partners 0.31 (0.14 to 0.66); unprotected anal sex with serodiscordant partners 0.34 (0.17 to 0.70); insertive unprotected 0.29 (0.14 to 0.58); receptive unprotected 0.27 (0.05 to 1.57), not significant.
key_findings.note: Counts are highly skewed (several SDs exceed three times the mean); these outcomes were not registered.

key_findings.finding: Depressive symptoms (CES-D) fell by 3.6 points overall (0.9 to 6.2) with no difference between arms (1.5 points, -3.7 to 6.7; p = .57); urine positivity was not associated with depression.
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in depression scores; Correlation of primary and secondary outcomes

key_findings.finding: Adverse events: no overall difference by arm (p >= .99); two serious events, neither judged drug-related (methamphetamine-induced paranoia on mirtazapine, vertebral fracture on placebo). Reported only on mirtazapine: drowsiness 13 of 30 (43%), increased appetite 4 (13%), weight gain 3 (10%; gains of 12.5, 9.5 and 7.9 kg); none stopped medication.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: drowsiness 13 of 30 versus 0 of 30, Fisher's exact p < 0.001, so specific adverse effects did differ by arm even though overall frequency did not.

key_findings.finding: Blinding check: 14 of 28 on placebo (50%) and 15 of 27 on mirtazapine (56%) guessed their assignment correctly (p = .79); guessing mirtazapine was not significantly associated with urine positivity (RR 0.76, 0.54 to 1.07).

Registration NCT00497081, first submitted 5 July 2007 as a feasibility pilot with feasibility, tolerability and acceptability primary outcomes; changed on 19 February 2008 (during recruitment) to efficacy, adherence and safety; respecified at results posting in October 2014. Registry results: 40% versus 6% reduction in positive urines from baseline to week 12; 109 versus 107 adverse events; one serious event per arm.
key_findings.page: ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT00497081 (current version and history versions 0, 2 and 8)
key_findings.locator: Outcome Measures; Study Record History; Results
key_findings.note: Read from the registry, not from the article; the article itself gives no registration number.

reporting_issues.issue: The article (author manuscript) does not state the trial registration number; the trial is registered as NCT00497081, whose original primary outcomes were feasibility, tolerability and acceptability, changed to efficacy during recruitment.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers of the article cannot see that the efficacy outcome was not the primary outcome at registration; the headline efficacy estimate should be read as from a trial first registered as a pilot.

reporting_issues.issue: Per-arm percentages are inconsistent with the counts: weekly urines are given as 84.9% (342 samples) for mirtazapine and 87.7% (331) for placebo, but 342 of 390 is 87.7% and 331 of 390 is 84.9%; raised ALT is given as 9 (23%) on mirtazapine and 7 (30%) on placebo, but 9 of 30 is 30% and 7 of 30 is 23%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The percentages appear swapped between arms in two places; which arm had more missing urines (and more raised ALT) cannot be stated with certainty from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The audio computer-assisted self-interview completion is given as 227 of 240, but the per-arm counts (113 and 112) sum to 225, and 112 of 120 is 93.3%, not the 95% printed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor arithmetic inconsistency in the secondary-outcome denominators.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1: the total for annual income of at least 40,000 dollars is 13 (22%), but the arms give 2 and 8 (total 10), and the income totals sum to 63 of 60; the row on history of self-help or treatment participation is labelled mean (SD) but contains counts and percentages (16 (53), 14 (47), 30 (50)).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical errors in the baseline table; they do not affect the primary analysis but the income imbalance is smaller in the total column than in the arms.

reporting_issues.issue: Screening flow: of 212 assessed in person, 110 were ineligible and 72 eligible, leaving 30 unaccounted for in the text (the flow diagram is an image).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; affects only the description of selection.

reporting_issues.issue: The power section expresses detectable effects as net reductions of 14 to 33 percentage points, and then compares them with an observed effect of 43%, which is the relative reduction implied by RR 0.57; the raw final-visit difference was about 19 percentage points (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim that the observed effect exceeded the detectable range mixes relative and absolute scales.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports no significant differences in adverse events by arm (p >= .99), while drowsiness (43%), increased appetite (13%) and weight gain (10%) were reported only in the mirtazapine arm.
reporting_issues.consequence: Overall adverse-event frequency hides a large specific difference (drowsiness p < 0.001, editors' calculation), which also bears on the plausibility of functional unblinding.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3437988 (NIH author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1 and 2 rendered as text, acknowledgments with funding and role of the sponsor, financial disclosure and reference list read; Figure 1 (flow) and Figure 2 (urine results by week) are images and their values were not extracted). Registration details, record history (versions 0, 2 and 8) and posted results additionally read from ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00497081.
